justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for the asset across all three horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 138.1 is essentially anchored to the last observed price with a very small upward drift, reflecting the assumption that short-term price momentum and market microstructure tend to produce mean-reverting but slightly trend-following behavior in liquid markets. At the one-week horizon, the estimate edges up to 138.8, incorporating a mild positive drift consistent with a modest risk premium or recent trend continuation. At the one-month horizon, the estimate rises further to 140.5, reflecting a longer-run fundamental or trend-based view that the asset has slightly more room to appreciate over that timeframe, possibly supported by macro conditions or sector dynamics that were prevailing at the time of the forecast.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is expected and reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only about 5.8 points, consistent with typical daily volatility for a moderately volatile asset. By one week, the interval widens to roughly 11.6 points, and by one month it spans 25 points, reflecting not just statistical volatility scaling with the square root of time but also the growing influence of regime-level uncertainties — things like shifts in monetary policy expectations, earnings surprises, or macroeconomic data that become more relevant at longer horizons. Liquidity conditions and the possibility of correlated market moves also contribute to fatter tails at longer horizons.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden risk-off episode triggered by geopolitical escalation, an unexpected central bank policy shift, or a systemic financial stress event could easily breach the lower bounds, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons. A negative earnings shock or sector-specific regulatory news could similarly cause a sharp drawdown. On the upside, a strongly positive macro surprise — such as a better-than-expected inflation print enabling rate cuts, or a significant positive catalyst specific to this asset — could push prices through the upper bounds. My intervals are calibrated around a base case, and tail events by definition fall outside them; the 10% of outcomes excluded by the 90% CI represent genuinely plausible but lower-probability scenarios that I would not dismiss.
